props.title: Dark Habits

sections.content: Pedro Almodóvar's Dark Habits (1983) marks a crucial early entry in his provocative filmography, diving into the twisted world of a convent harboring bizarre secrets. Like Luis Buñuel's Viridiana (1961), it skewers religious hypocrisy through dark comedy, following a cabaret singer seeking refuge among nuns with decidedly un-nunlike vices. The film establishes Almodóvar's signature blend of melodrama, camp, and social critique that would later flourish in Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown (1988) and All About My Mother (1999).

sections.content: Almodóvar's treatment of religious themes through a transgressive lens connects to a rich tradition of provocative convent films. Ken Russell's The Devils (1971) pushed boundaries with its explicit critique of religious and political corruption, while Cristian Mungiu's Beyond the Hills (2012) offered a stark, realist examination of faith and obsession. Dark Habits distinguishes itself through its uniquely Spanish perspective, mixing Catholic imagery with post-Franco liberation. SUBHEAD: Breaking Traditional Religious Cinema

Unlike reverential religious films like The Nun's Story (1959), Dark Habits deliberately subverts expectations through its outrageous characters and plot turns. Each nun represents a different vice or obsession - from drug addiction to erotic writing - creating a microcosm of repressed desires erupting through religious facade. This approach influenced later works like Paul Verhoeven's Benedetta (2021), which similarly explores power, sexuality, and faith within convent walls.
